analogy.p: Imagine a school where all the water for drinks is in one big jug at one end of the canteen (the surplus area), while most of the pupils are queuing at the other end (the deficit area). Supply is the jug, demand is the number of thirsty pupils, and a water transfer is a teacher carrying the jug or a long pipe that moves water to where the crowd is. Water stress is when the jug runs low because too many pupils want a drink. The analogy breaks down because real water supplies are renewed by rainfall that varies by season and year, and moving real water over long distances costs a great deal and affects people and ecosystems along the way.
analogy.t: A school canteen with one big water jug

bullets: **Water supply** = the amount of usable fresh water available in a place from rainfall, rivers, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater.
**Water demand** = the amount of water people, farms and industry want or use in a place; it is measured as water used per person per day or per year.
**Water surplus** = supply is greater than demand; **water deficit** = demand is greater than supply.
**Water insecurity** = when people cannot reliably get enough safe, clean water for drinking, sanitation, food and a healthy life.
**Water transfer** = moving water from a place of surplus to a place of deficit by pipeline, canal, tunnel or river.
Always link your answer to a place or data: examiners reward developed points such as 'because the south east has low rainfall but a large population, demand is higher than supply'.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA wants you to understand **water supply and demand** and why they are unevenly matched across the world and within the UK. You must be able to explain what makes a place have a **water surplus** or a **water deficit**, how **water insecurity** arises, what its **causes and impacts** are, and how **water transfer** moves water from places with plenty to places that need it. This is part of the 'challenge of resource management' unit on Paper 2, where you study food, water or energy, and exam questions on water often use a map, a graph or a short case study to test whether you can interpret data and then explain it.

bullets: An **aquifer** is a layer of permeable rock (such as chalk or sandstone) that holds groundwater; it can be tapped by wells and boreholes.
**Surface water** (rivers, lakes, reservoirs) is easy to reach but is lost to evaporation and is easily polluted.
**Groundwater** is stored underground and is slow to replenish; if it is pumped faster than it refills it is being **over-abstracted**.
Water-rich areas include the tropical rainforests and cool temperate areas with reliable rain, such as parts of northern Europe, Canada and the Amazon basin.
Water-poor areas include hot deserts and semi-arid areas such as North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and parts of Australia and the south-west of the USA.
Do not say 'there is not enough water in the world': the problem is the **uneven distribution** of usable water compared with where people live and what they use it for.
core.h: Where water comes from: the global picture
core.p: Roughly **97% of the water on Earth is salt water** in oceans, so only about **3% is fresh water**, and most of that is locked up as ice in glaciers and ice sheets or lies deep underground as groundwater. The share that people can easily use, in rivers, lakes, shallow groundwater and rainfall, is tiny. Fresh water is renewed by the **water cycle** (evaporation, condensation, precipitation and runoff), so supply in any place depends on rainfall, how quickly water runs off or soaks in, and how much is stored in lakes, reservoirs and aquifers. Because rainfall is not spread evenly, some countries are water-rich and others are water-poor.

bullets: **Population growth** means more people drinking, washing, cooking and needing food grown with irrigation.
**Economic development** raises industrial use (manufacturing, cooling in power stations, mining) and household use (showers, toilets, appliances, gardens).
**Changing lifestyles** in NEEs and HICs increase water use per person: a typical UK person uses roughly 140 to 150 litres a day at home, far more than many people in LICs.
**Agriculture** takes the largest share of water globally; irrigated farming in dry areas can use a huge amount of water per hectare.
**Water footprint (virtual water)**: the hidden water used to make a product, such as the water used to grow cotton for a T-shirt or feed for beef.
**Urbanisation** concentrates demand in cities, which often have to bring water in from a long way away.
Link to other topics: urban growth in NEEs, development indicators, climate change and agricultural change on Paper 2.
core.h: Water demand: why it keeps rising
core.p: World demand for water has risen faster than population because richer, more urban societies use far more water per person. The biggest user globally is **agriculture**, mostly for irrigation, followed by industry and then households. Demand rises when there are **more people**, when **incomes rise** (people buy washing machines, dishwashers and cars, and eat more meat, which needs a lot of water to produce), and when **industry and energy generation** expand. Demand is also affected by **climate** (hot dry places irrigate more) and by **how efficiently water is used and priced**.

bullets: **Water stress**: demand starts to exceed the supply that is available or the quality is too poor; below about 1,700 m³ per person per year.
**Water scarcity**: below about 1,000 m³ per person per year, shortages happen regularly.
**Absolute scarcity**: below about 500 m³ per person per year; there is not enough water to meet basic needs without outside help.
Formula: water per person = total renewable water available divided by population.
A country's average hides differences: a wet rainy season and a dry season, or rich and poor households, can mean some people are short even when the national average looks adequate.
Graph tip: when asked to describe a map of water stress, name the continents or regions with the highest stress, quote figures if given, and mention anomalies.
core.h: Measuring water supply: stress and scarcity
core.p: Geographers compare water supply with population using the amount of **renewable water per person per year**, measured in **cubic metres (m³)**. A commonly used scale (the Falkenmark indicator) says that a country with more than about **1,700 m³ per person per year** has adequate supply, below that it experiences **water stress**, below **1,000 m³** it has **water scarcity**, and below **500 m³** it faces **absolute scarcity**. These numbers are useful because they combine supply and demand: a country with plenty of rain but a huge population can still be stressed. Always use the units 'cubic metres per person per year' and state whether the figure is above or below the thresholds.

bullets: Physical scarcity is typical of **deserts and semi-arid areas** such as the Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia.
Economic scarcity is common in parts of **sub-Saharan Africa** and South Asia, where rivers exist but pipes, pumps and treatment plants are missing.
A country can have both: for example a dry area where the poorest people cannot afford the water that is available.
**Water quality** also limits supply: polluted water (from sewage, industry or farm chemicals) is not safe, so the usable supply is smaller than the total volume.
Climate change is expected to make dry places drier and rainfall less reliable, adding to physical scarcity in some regions.
Use the terms 'physical' and 'economic' in an answer, and give a reason for each.
core.p: There are two main reasons a place can be short of water. **Physical (natural) water scarcity** happens where there is simply not enough water to meet demand, usually because the climate is dry or because the population is very large for the water available. **Economic water scarcity** happens where the water exists, for example in rivers, aquifers or lakes, but people cannot get it because they lack the **money, technology and infrastructure** to store, treat and pipe it. Understanding the difference matters because the solutions are different: dry places may need to move or save water, while economically scarce places need investment in wells, pipes and sanitation.

bullets: **Climate and drought**: low, unreliable or seasonal rainfall, and long dry periods, reduce supply; climate change can make this worse.
**Over-abstraction**: taking water from rivers or aquifers faster than rainfall refills them lowers river flow and the water table.
**Pollution**: sewage, industrial waste and agricultural chemicals make water unsafe, which reduces the amount that can be used.
**Population growth and urbanisation** increase demand in cities and put pressure on local sources.
**Poor infrastructure**: leaking pipes, no storage and no treatment mean water is lost or unsafe; in poor areas water may have to be carried from far away.
**Poverty and lack of investment** (economic scarcity) mean people cannot afford wells, taps or water treatment.
**Conflict and politics**: water shared by several countries, such as the Nile or the Tigris-Euphrates, can lead to disputes over dams and abstraction.
core.h: Causes of water deficit and insecurity
core.p: Water insecurity usually has several causes working together. **Natural causes** include low or highly seasonal rainfall and drought. **Human causes** include rising demand, **over-abstraction** of rivers and aquifers, **pollution** of rivers and groundwater, and **poor management** such as leaking pipes. Political and economic factors matter too: rivers often cross borders, so an upstream country can reduce what reaches a downstream country, and poorer countries may not be able to afford dams, pipes or treatment works. In an exam, the best answers choose two or three causes and **explain the link** to deficit rather than just listing them.

bullets: **Health**: waterborne diseases (cholera, typhoid, dysentery), diarrhoea, dehydration and poor hygiene due to lack of water for washing.
**Food**: crop failure and livestock death reduce food supply, leading to undernutrition and higher food prices.
**Economic**: industries and power stations that need water have to slow down or close; time lost fetching water reduces working hours; farmers lose income.
**Social**: children, especially girls, miss school to collect water; water shortages can cause migration from rural to urban areas and to other countries.
**Conflict**: disputes over shared rivers and over access to wells and boreholes can lead to local or international tension.
**Environmental**: rivers and lakes shrink, wetlands dry out and wildlife loses habitat; in the Aral Sea region over-use of rivers for irrigation caused the sea to shrink dramatically.
Make your answer clear by explaining **how** one impact leads to another (a chain), for example drought, then crop failure, then food shortage, then higher prices.
core.p: The impacts of too little clean water affect **health, food, the economy, society and the environment**, and each can make the others worse. Without safe water people suffer **waterborne diseases** such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery, which spread through contaminated water and poor sanitation and are a major cause of illness and death in young children. Lack of water also reduces crop yields and livestock, leading to **food shortages** and rising food prices, and in the worst cases famine. Time spent collecting water, often by women and girls, reduces school attendance and income. These impacts then feed back into more poverty, which keeps economic water scarcity going.

bullets: **Surplus areas** (north and west): higher rainfall, upland catchments good for reservoirs, lower population density.
**Deficit areas** (south and east): lower rainfall, high evaporation in summer, high population density and large urban demand, especially London.
**Supply sources** in the UK: reservoirs, rivers, and groundwater from aquifers such as the chalk beneath south east England.
**Demand** comes from households, industry, farming and power generation; household use averages roughly 140 to 150 litres per person per day.
**Seasonal variation**: demand peaks in hot dry summers (gardens, showers) just when supply is lowest, which can lead to hosepipe bans.
**Leakage** from ageing pipes wastes a large amount of treated water, adding to the supply problem.
Link to other topics: relief rainfall and UK weather (Paper 1), population distribution and London (Paper 2).
core.h: Water supply and demand in the UK
core.p: The UK is a wet country overall but its water is unevenly spread. The **north and west** (Scotland, Wales, north-west England) have high rainfall because of the upland relief (relief rainfall) and relatively few people, so they have a **water surplus**. The **south and east** (especially London and the south east) have lower rainfall, flatter land and a very large and growing population, so demand is high and they have a **water deficit**. This mismatch is the main reason water has to be moved around the country. Demand is also rising with population growth, new housing and higher use per person, and climate change may make summer rainfall less reliable.

bullets: **Pipelines and aqueducts** carry water by gravity downhill or with pumps uphill; pumping needs energy and increases cost.

**River transfers**: water is released from an upland reservoir into a river, then abstracted downstream by a town; Kielder Water in Northumberland, for example, is used to support supply to the Tyne, Wear and Tees areas.
The **Elan Valley aqueduct** in Wales, built over a century ago, carries water by gravity to Birmingham, an example of a UK long-distance transfer.
Transfers need **water treatment works** to make the water safe before it enters homes.

Large international or national examples include the **Lesotho Highlands Water Project** (water from Lesotho to the Gauteng region of South Africa) and the **South-North Water Transfer Project** in China, which aims to take water from the wetter south to the drier, populous north.
The key idea is moving water from where it is **plentiful** to where it is **needed**.
core.h: Water transfer: the idea and how it works
core.p: A **water transfer scheme** takes water from a place with a surplus (the **donor area**) to a place with a deficit (the **recipient area**). It usually involves a **reservoir** in a wet upland area, a **dam** to store the water, and a system of **pipelines, canals, tunnels or an existing river channel** to carry the water. The water is then treated and supplied to homes and industry. Transfers can be small, within a region, or huge, between river basins or even countries. Because they involve building engineering structures and moving large volumes, they are expensive and have social and environmental effects.

bullets: **Advantage**: provides large, reliable supply to deficit areas and allows economic growth and population growth in dry regions.
**Advantage**: dams can provide **HEP**, control flooding and allow irrigation, giving multiple benefits.
**Disadvantage**: very **expensive** to build and maintain; LICs may need loans, increasing debt.
**Disadvantage**: people can be **displaced** when valleys are flooded, and farmland, forests and archaeology can be lost.
**Disadvantage**: **ecosystems** are harmed; fish are blocked, sediment is trapped behind the dam, and downstream flow and water quality decrease.
**Disadvantage**: can cause **conflict** when donor areas feel they lose out, or when rivers cross borders.
**Evaluation**: whether a scheme is 'worth it' depends on who is affected, on the scale, on alternatives (conservation, desalination), and on sustainability in the long term.
core.h: Advantages and disadvantages of water transfer and dams
core.p: Water transfer can solve shortages, but it has costs and conflicts. The **advantages** are that it gives a large and reliable supply to a deficit area, supports cities and industry, and can bring extra benefits such as **hydroelectric power**, **flood control** and recreation. The **disadvantages** include high construction and running costs, **loss of land and homes** under the reservoir, **damage to ecosystems and fish migration**, reduced river flow downstream, and tensions between regions or countries over who owns the water. A good answer weighs both sides and reaches a judgement, not just a list.

bullets: **Demand management**: metering, tariffs, hosepipe bans, leak repair, water-saving fittings, and education.
**Desalination** produces fresh water from sea water but needs a lot of energy and is expensive; it is used in dry coastal countries such as Saudi Arabia and Israel.
**Groundwater abstraction** uses boreholes to pump from aquifers; over-use lowers the water table and may let salt water enter near the coast.
**Recycling** treated waste water, for example Singapore's NEWater, reduces the need for new supply.
Sustainable management means meeting present needs **without reducing the ability of future generations** to meet theirs.
Link to other topics: energy needs (desalination, pumping), food (irrigation) and climate change.
core.h: Managing the demand side and alternative sources
core.p: Moving water around is only one answer; **reducing demand** and using other sources can be cheaper and more sustainable. Water companies encourage households to use less through **metering** (so people pay for what they use), **water-efficient appliances**, repairing leaks, and public campaigns. Industry and farming can reuse water and use **drip irrigation**. Other sources include **groundwater abstraction**, **desalination** (removing salt from sea water) and **recycling waste water**. These strategies are examined in more detail in the next specification point on increasing supply sustainably, but you should be able to compare them with transfer.

bullets: **Describe** the pattern: for example 'water stress is highest in North Africa and the Middle East, and lowest in northern Europe and Canada'.
**Quote data**: use figures and units, and use 'about' for readings from a graph; use comparisons such as 'twice as high as'.
**Anomalies**: mention a country that does not fit the pattern, for example a wet country with high stress because of a large population.
**Calculations**: total water divided by population gives water per person; compare with the thresholds.
**Percentage change**: (change divided by original) multiplied by 100 is often needed with demand data.
Always finish a data answer by **explaining** at least one reason, even if the question says 'describe', if marks allow.
core.h: Interpreting maps and data on water
core.p: Exam questions often give a **choropleth map**, a **bar chart** or a **table** of water availability, usage or stress and ask you to describe patterns or compare places. A good description names the pattern, quotes data with units, and mentions exceptions. A good explanation gives the reason, linking rainfall, population, development and management. Practise using terms like 'water stress', 'surplus' and 'deficit' with the data, and always include units such as litres per person per day or cubic metres per person per year.

bullets: **Link to development**: access to clean water and sanitation is a key indicator of development and a UN Sustainable Development Goal.
**Link to food**: irrigation uses most of the world's fresh water, so water shortages cause food shortages.
**Link to energy**: hydro-electric dams generate power, but pumping and desalination use energy.
**Link to climate**: global warming changes rainfall patterns and glacier melt, which affects river flow.
**Command words**: 'describe' = say what; 'explain' = say why; 'assess' = weigh up and reach a judgement; 'to what extent' = give a balanced view and conclude.
**Use place-specific detail** (a named reservoir, scheme or country) to reach the top levels in extended answers.
If unsure of a figure, use words like 'about' or 'roughly' rather than inventing an exact number.
core.h: Linking water to other topics and exam skills
core.p: Water links to food (irrigation), energy (hydro-electric power, cooling and pumping), health and development (clean water and sanitation) and climate change (changing rainfall). Examiners reward answers that make these links and that use specific named places. For the resource management unit you study **one** of food, water or energy in detail, so check which one your school taught, but the ideas of supply, demand, security and sustainability are common to all three and can be compared.

exam: 1 mark 'state' or 'give' questions: write one precise fact, for example one cause of water deficit such as drought or over-abstraction.
2 mark 'describe' questions on a map or graph: name the pattern, quote data with units, and add a comparison or anomaly.
2 to 3 mark 'explain' questions: make a point, then add a developed reason using 'because' or 'which means'; each developed point earns a mark.

4 mark 'explain why' questions on the UK: contrast north and west (high rainfall, upland, few people, surplus) with south and east (low rainfall, many people, deficit) and state that this creates the need for transfer.
Calculations: show the formula (water per person = total divided by population), the working, the answer, and the units.
Use the correct terms: water supply, demand, surplus, deficit, stress, scarcity, insecurity, abstraction, aquifer, reservoir, transfer.
6 mark 'assess' or 'to what extent' questions: give advantages, disadvantages, and a clear final judgement supported by evidence, with a named scheme.
Use named examples and places (for example Kielder Water, the Elan Valley aqueduct, the Lesotho Highlands Water Project) with specific facts rather than general statements.
Data tip: read the axis labels and units, use 'about' for graph values, and compare at least two places.
Always read the command word and the mark allocation, and aim for roughly one clear point per mark.

mistakes.r: There is enough in total; the problem is uneven distribution of usable fresh water compared with where people live and use it.
mistakes.w: There is not enough water in the world.

mistakes.r: HICs can have deficits too, for example south east England, where demand is high compared with rainfall and supply.
mistakes.w: Water deficit only happens in LICs.

mistakes.r: Water stress is when supply per person is below about 1,700 cubic metres per year and demand starts to exceed supply.
Physical = not enough water exists; economic = water exists but people cannot afford or access it.
mistakes.w: Physical and economic scarcity mean the same.

mistakes.r: Give advantages and disadvantages (cost, displacement, ecosystem damage, conflict) and reach a judgement.
mistakes.w: Water transfers are always good because they bring water to people.

mistakes.r: The UK has a surplus in the north and west and a deficit in the south and east, so transfers are needed.
mistakes.w: The UK has plenty of water everywhere.

mistakes.r: Write '1,200 cubic metres per person per year' and compare it with the stress thresholds.
mistakes.w: Giving a figure with no unit, such as 1,200.

mistakes.r: Link each point with 'because', 'which leads to', so the chain of cause and effect is explained.

summary: AQA expects you to explain how and why water supply and demand are mismatched globally and in the UK, to describe the causes and impacts of water deficit and insecurity, and to explain how water transfer moves water from surplus to deficit areas. It matters because water security underpins health, food and economic development.

terms.d: The amount of usable fresh water available in a place from rainfall, rivers, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater.
The amount of water that people, farming and industry want or use in a place.
When water supply is greater than demand.
When water demand is greater than supply.
When people do not have reliable access to enough safe, clean water for drinking, sanitation, food and health.
When the amount of water available is below about 1,700 cubic metres per person per year, so demand starts to exceed supply.
When the amount of water available falls below about 1,000 cubic metres per person per year.
A shortage because there is not enough water in the area to meet demand, usually from a dry climate or large population.
A shortage because people lack the money, technology or infrastructure to get water that exists.
A layer of permeable rock that stores groundwater.
Taking water from a river or aquifer faster than it is replaced.
Moving water from an area of surplus to an area of deficit, by pipeline, canal, tunnel or river.
A large artificial lake behind a dam used to store water.
An illness spread by drinking or using contaminated water, such as cholera or typhoid.
The total volume of water used to produce the goods and services a person or country uses.
Using water so that present needs are met without stopping future generations from meeting theirs.

worked.ans: **1,200 cubic metres per person per year**, which is below 1,700, so the country faces **water stress** (but not scarcity).
worked.q: A country has a population of 40 million and its total renewable water resources are 48 billion cubic metres per year. Calculate the water available per person per year and state whether the country faces water stress. (3 marks)
steps: Water per person = total water divided by population.
48 000 000 000 divided by 40 000 000 = 1,200 cubic metres per person per year.
Compare with thresholds: 1,200 is below 1,700 (stress) but above 1,000 (scarcity).

worked.q: A household of 4 people each uses 140 litres of water a day. Calculate the household's total water use in a year in cubic metres. (2 marks)
steps: 1 cubic metre = 1,000 litres, so 204,400 divided by 1,000 = 204.4 cubic metres.

worked.ans: The south east has **lower rainfall** but **very high demand** because of its large population, especially London, and demand peaks in dry summers. This means demand exceeds the local supply, creating a **water deficit** that may need to be met by abstraction from aquifers or **water transfer** from wetter areas.
worked.q: Explain why parts of the south east of England have a water deficit, even though the UK is a wet country. (4 marks)
steps: Point 1: the south east has lower rainfall than the north and west because it is lower and flatter and further from the wet Atlantic weather.
Point 2: it has a high population density and a large city (London), so total demand is very high.
Point 3: demand is greatest in summer when rainfall and river flow are lowest, so supply cannot meet demand.
Point 4: there are few large upland reservoir sites, so water may need to be abstracted from groundwater or transferred.
